# Designing for the Heat: How Cities Can Make Summer Bearable

Summer in the modern city has become a hazard to be survived rather than a season to be enjoyed. As climate change pushes temperatures higher and heat waves grow longer and more frequent, urban areas suffer disproportionately: asphalt and concrete absorb sunlight all day and release it slowly at night, buildings block cooling breezes, and cars pump out exhaust heat. The result is the urban heat island effect, in which city centers can run several degrees hotter than surrounding countryside—sometimes as much as ten degrees on still nights. Yet the heat is not evenly distributed. It falls hardest on neighborhoods with few trees, aging housing, and residents who cannot afford air conditioning. The central argument of this essay is that urban heat is not primarily a natural phenomenon but a design failure, and that the remedies—trees, thoughtful street design, better housing, and robust public transit—are well understood. The real challenge is navigating the tradeoffs these remedies demand, because making a city cooler requires choices about money, space, and whose comfort gets prioritized.

Trees are the most intuitive and among the most effective tools. A mature street tree does several things at once: its canopy shades pavement that would otherwise absorb and reradiate heat, its leaves transpire moisture that cools the surrounding air, and its presence makes walking outside feel psychologically bearable. Studies consistently find that shaded streets can be several degrees cooler than exposed ones, and shaded surfaces can be dramatically cooler to the touch. The city of Medellín, Colombia, offers the most celebrated example. Beginning in 2016, the city built a network of thirty "green corridors," planting trees and vegetation along heavily trafficked roads and waterways. Within a few years, the corridors had cooled the city by around two degrees Celsius, while also improving air quality and attracting birds and pedestrians back to streets that had been hostile corridors of traffic. In the United States, cities such as Sacramento and New York have run long-standing tree-planting programs, and Phoenix—America's hottest large city—has committed to a goal of tree canopy covering a quarter of the city by 2030.

The problem is that trees are not free, and they are not distributed fairly. A canopy takes a decade or more to mature, requires irrigation in dry climates, and can crack sidewalks and sewer lines if poorly sited. In arid cities like Phoenix, the water cost of a large canopy is a genuine ethical question in a region facing long-term drought. More troubling is the distributional pattern: in most American cities, tree cover maps almost perfectly onto historical maps of redlining. Neighborhoods that were denied mortgage investment in the mid-twentieth century remain the hottest today, with sparse canopies and abundant pavement. When cities finally plant trees in these neighborhoods, they can inadvertently trigger "green gentrification"—rising property values and rents that push out the very residents the trees were meant to protect. The lesson is that tree planting must be paired with housing policy, or the cooling benefit becomes a displacement mechanism.

Street design is the second lever, and it interacts closely with trees. Wide, straight streets lined with dark asphalt and flanked by glass towers function like ovens. Narrower streets, lighter-colored pavements, and buildings that shade sidewalks can dramatically reduce surface temperatures. Los Angeles has pioneered "cool pavement" coatings that reflect rather than absorb sunlight, lowering surface temperatures by ten degrees or more on treated blocks, though residents sometimes complain about glare and the fact that reflected heat can make a person standing on the street feel warmer. Barcelona's "superblocks" scheme offers a more radical redesign: clusters of city blocks are closed to through traffic, and the reclaimed street space is turned into plazas, playgrounds, and plantings. The superblocks have reduced traffic, noise, and heat while creating genuinely pleasant public space—though they have also drawn protests from drivers and businesses worried about access, and questions about whether the improvements will raise rents in the surrounding blocks.

The most important street-design decision, however, is how much space to give to cars. Automobiles are heat machines: they generate waste heat directly, and the infrastructure they demand—parking lots, wide lanes, highways—replaces vegetation with heat-absorbing surfaces. Every parking lot is a miniature desert. Cities that reclaim even a fraction of that space for trees, shade structures, or permeable surfaces reap immediate cooling benefits. But this is where tradeoffs become sharpest. Residents and businesses often fight the loss of parking, and delivery drivers, people with disabilities, and tradespeople have legitimate needs for vehicle access. The honest answer is that a cooler city is a city that is, in some respects, less convenient for drivers. That is a real cost, and it should be acknowledged rather than dismissed.

Housing is the third frontier, and arguably the most urgent, because heat kills people indoors. In Phoenix, most heat deaths occur indoors, in homes where residents cannot afford to run air conditioning or where the building itself offers no protection. Older apartment buildings with flat dark roofs, poor insulation, and single-pane windows become heat traps. Simple retrofits—reflective "cool roofs," insulation, window shading, and heat pumps—can transform a dangerous apartment into a survivable one. New York City's CoolRoofs program has coated millions of square feet of rooftops with reflective paint, and cities from Ahmedabad to Athens have launched programs to weatherize the housing of low-income residents. The deeper issue is that building codes have long been written for cold-weather performance, prioritizing heating efficiency over cooling. Updating codes to require passive cooling—cross-ventilation, external shading, light-colored walls, and operable windows—would make new housing safer by design. The tradeoff, again, is cost: retrofits are expensive, and landlords pass costs to tenants unless subsidies intervene. Treating cooling as a public utility, the way heating assistance has long been treated, is a policy choice cities must make.

Public transit, finally, is both a cooling strategy and a heat-vulnerability problem. Every bus rider is a person not driving a car, so good transit reduces the heat a city generates. But transit riders wait outside, often at stops with no shade, and heat waves make transit use punishing. Cities that take heat seriously treat bus stops as infrastructure worth investing in: shaded shelters, drinking fountains, and real-time arrival information that lets people wait indoors. Los Angeles, after years of criticism for its sparse shelters, has begun building thousands of them. Some cities have experimented with "cooling buses" or air-conditioned public buildings designated as refuge centers during heat emergencies. The tradeoff here is between speed and comfort: dedicated bus lanes make transit faster and more attractive, but they consume road space, provoking the same political fights
